# Transformer Roofline + FP32→FP16 Drill

[← Microsoft](../README.md) · [Every Microsoft question](../../microsoft.md) · [Read it on TrueInterview](https://trueinterview.io/study/transformer-roofline-fp-precision)

`arithmetic-intensity` `gpu` `kernel` `numerical-stability` `transformer`

---

## Requirements

The MAI infrastructure loop has four rounds and no LeetCode component. Each session lasts about 45 minutes following a brief resume exercise:

**Round 1 — Resume / project pressure-test.** This follows the usual MAI deep-dive format: choose one infrastructure project and justify both your ownership and your trade-offs.

**Round 2 — Transformer code review + roofline.** Explain a small transformer block as the interviewer follows along. With matrix dimensions `(M, K)·(K, N)` and the GPU's maximum FLOPs and HBM bandwidth, calculate the **arithmetic intensity** `2·M·N·K / (bytes moved)` and the **roofline time bound** — the workload is memory-bound if intensity is below peak/bandwidth, and compute-bound otherwise. Be prepared to perform the dimensional analysis verbally and put the result on the board.

**Round 3 — CUDA vibe-coding.** Launch your IDE and use an AI-coding assistant of your choice (Cursor / Copilot / Claude Code) to create a small CUDA kernel for matmul or reduction. The assessment focuses on how naturally you work with the assistant rather than on hand-writing kernels. Candidates who lacked a prepared AI environment have been penalized.

**Round 4 — Residual connections + FP32→FP16 cast.** On the whiteboard, derive the gradient for `y = x + f(x)` and explain how the identity path preserves gradient flow (`∂L/∂x = ∂L/∂y · (1 + f'(x))`). Then explain which FP16 cast locations cause problems — usually, small gradients in deep layers underflow; mixed-precision training retains master weights in FP32 and converts to lower precision only for the forward / backward matmul.

## Notes

The roofline model to remember is: time ≈ max(compute\_time, memory\_time), with `compute_time = FLOPs / peak_TFLOPS` and `memory_time = bytes / bandwidth`. For matrix multiplication, FLOPs = `2·M·N·K`, while bytes ≈ `2·(M·K + K·N + M·N)` with FP16. On an A100 (312 TF FP16, 1.5 TB/s HBM), a $$4096\times 4096\times 4096$$ matmul is compute-bound, whereas a tall-and-skinny $$4096\times 1\times 4096$$ operation is bandwidth-bound — interviewers expect you to recognize the effect of shape.

Mixed-precision issues to mention when asked include gradient underflow → loss scaling; the epsilon in the layernorm denominator → retain it in FP32; and matmul accumulators → use FP32 (`bf16` avoids this particular issue because its exponent range is wider).

For the residual-connection explanation, the `(1 + f'(x))` term in the gradient prevents the lower bound from reaching zero even when `f` becomes arbitrarily deep, which is the fundamental reason for ResNet-style skip paths in Transformer feed-forward and attention layers.

## Preparation

- Commit the peak FP16 TFLOPS and HBM bandwidth figures for A100, H100, and your target hardware to memory; interviewers want concrete values rather than vague orders of magnitude.
- Set up your IDE for AI-supported coding **before the loop**. Rehearse a 10-minute kernel-writing exercise the evening beforehand until the tools feel automatic.
- Practice deriving the residual gradient on paper; this prompt comes up repeatedly in infrastructure deep-dives.
- Study mixed-precision training (loss scaling, master weights, and BF16 versus FP16 trade-offs) until you can state the difference in two sentences.
